newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK legislators vow to defy new curbs on protests.
newsitem.headline: HK legislators vow to defy new curbs on protests.

text.p: Pro-democracy legislators vowed on Sunday to march in protest just minutes after Hong Kong's July 1 handover to China, refusing to recognize new limits on demonstrations coming into effect that day.

Members of the Frontier political alliance also promised to avenge Beijing's decision to scrap Hong Kong's elected legislature by winning new polls promised within a year of the British colony's return to Chinese rule.

Legislator Emily Lau said Frontier and other activist groups would hold a pro-democracy rally on the evening of June 30 and then march on government offices in the first minutes of July 1 after it passes to Chinese rule at midnight.
"We will be carrying torches, huge flames to show the flames of democracy," she told a news conference.
Fellow Frontier legislator Lee Cheuk-yan said the group would notify police of their plans, as required by current law.
But it would not seek a "notice of no objection" as required under new laws to be enacted by the controversial provisional legislature that will replace the current council, he said.

"On the question of whether we will apply for a permit to march on July 1, we will definitely do so," Lee said. "We will use the same notification form that we have used in the past because we do not recognize the new law."
Pro-democracy activists have denounced the new laws as a de facto permit system designed to stifle dissent.
Hong Kong's future leader, Tung Chee-hwa, made clear on Sunday that the new laws would have effect the minute the territory becomes a part of China on July 1.

Lau said Frontier would not be joining the Democratic Party, Hong Kong's largest, which plans to denounce the new provisional legislature from balcony of the Legislative Council building in central Hong Kong just after the handover.
Hong Kong's Legislative Council was fully elected for the first time ever in polls held in 1995.

But Beijing said electoral rules for the 1995 polls violated previous Sino-British accords and decided to replace the legislature on July 1 with a provisional council hand-picked by a China-backed committee, promising fresh elections under revised rules within a year of Hong Kong's handover.
Lau said Frontier would work together with the rest of Hong Kong's democratic camp and go all out to win those polls.

"We hope to get the Hong Kong people's support and to show China, to show the Hong Kong people and the international community, that the pro-democracy movement has the support of the majority of the Hong Kong people," she said.

Frontier's five current legislators said they faced many limitations. Once out of office they would have a harder time raising funds and getting media attention, and new electoral rules are expected to favour pro-Beijing candidates, they said.
But legislator and labour activist Lau Chin-shek vowed to make a mark.
"Within the limitations, we will get the largest success," he said. "I can guarantee to everybody that we will win."
